conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood.

Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me there’s an immediate safety concern.

I’ll ask each question just the way it’s written, and all I need is the answer that feels most true for you over the past seven days. We’ll go one question at a time, and we can pause whenever you need.

Let’s start:

Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
No… not really. I mean, maybe once or twice something small made me smile, but mostly I just feel too tired and heavy inside to laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Definitely not as much as I used to. I’ll catch myself forcing a little chuckle if someone tries to joke, but it feels fake and fades right away. Nothing really feels funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels flat. I’ll think “I should want to do that,” but I can’t stir up any real enthusiasm.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes… most of the time. If the baby won’t settle or I’m running late, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m just not good enough at this mom thing. I keep replaying it in my head and beating myself up, even when I know, rationally, it’s not all my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, quite a lot. Even when everything seems okay, I keep imagining something awful might happen—like the baby could stop breathing or I’ll drop him, or I’m missing some sign that he’s sick. My mind just races and I can’t settle it, even when there’s no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It’s not every day, but a few times this week I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. Nothing’s happening—no noise, no problem—it just rises up out of nowhere and I have to remind myself I’m safe.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most of the time. Between the night feedings, the crying I can’t always soothe, and just trying to keep us both fed and clean, I feel like I’m drowning. Some mornings I don’t want to get out of bed because I already know I won’t be able to keep up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes, most of the time. I lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning with everything I think I did wrong that day and all the “what-ifs” about the baby. I’ll drift off for a bit and then jerk awake for no reason, and after that I can’t settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, most of the time. It’s like a weight sitting on my chest. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I just feel empty or like I’m about to cry. Even when I try to “snap out of it,” the sadness sticks around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, most of the time. I’ve ended up in tears almost every day this week—sometimes when the baby won’t settle, sometimes when I’m staring at the mess in the kitchen and feel too tired to clean it, and sometimes for no clear reason at all. The tears just come and I can’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the joy you expected after birth feels gone-laughter and plans feel flat, replaced by a heavy sadness that shows up most of every day. You describe feeling overwhelmed, crying easily, blaming yourself for normal baby challenges, and being bombarded by racing "what-if" worries even when things are quiet. Yet you have also been clear that you have no thoughts of harming yourself, which is important and reassuring.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports total loss of ability to enjoy humor, forcing fake laughter that fades instantly</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as "flat" and lacking enthusiasm, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "most of the time" and describes pervasive self-blame for routine infant-care issues, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries occurring "quite a lot" with vivid catastrophic images and inability to settle, aligning with "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of panic with racing heart and breathlessness multiple times in the week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient says "most of the time" and describes feeling overwhelmed, "drowning," and unable to keep up, matching the highest distress option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Yes, most of the time" and describes classic insomnia—racing thoughts, frequent awakenings, and inability to return to sleep—matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "most of the time" plus persistent emptiness and frequent crying, perfectly matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "most of the time" and "almost every day" which aligns with the highest frequency option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 on the EPDS places you well above the cut-off for probable major depression. You endorsed the highest severity option for eight of ten items, meeting core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, fatigue, and sleep disturbance. Frequent, intrusive worries and sudden physiologic panic suggest comorbid postpartum anxiety. No self-harm ideation was reported. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review results and discuss medication and therapy options
2. Ask about referral to a perinatal <med>mental health specialist</med> or psychiatrist experienced with <med>postpartum depression/anxiety</med>
3. Consider evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> tailored for the postpartum period
4. Enlist practical support-partner, family, friends, or a postpartum doula-to cover night shifts, meals, or household tasks so you can rest
5. Encourage 20-30 minutes of gentle outdoor activity or stroller walk daily if cleared by your clinician; light movement can modestly boost mood
6. Plan brief, scheduled "worry time" followed by a calming activity to reduce rumination when trying to sleep
7. Keep follow-up appointments and re-screen with EPDS or PHQ-9 in two weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report; responses consistent with moderate–severe distress.

Symptom Highlights  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of humor, anticipatory pleasure)  
- Pervasive low mood with daily tearfulness  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Persistent, intrusive “what-if” worries and nocturnal rumination  
- Episodic physiologic panic (heart racing, breathlessness) without clear trigger  
- Subjective sense of “drowning” and difficulty coping with routine tasks  
- Sleep initiation / maintenance problems linked to mood preoccupation  

Risk Indicators  
- All core affective items endorsed “most of the time”  
- Anxiety items endorsed “quite a lot / sometimes”  
- No self-harm ideation reported (denied on Q10)

Screening Impression  
Responses place patient above standard cut-off for probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; significant functional impairment and emotional distress evident. Safety risk appears limited to mood disturbance without self-harm intent. Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialty for comprehensive evaluation and discussion of treatment options.
